description_full: Sasol Limited operates as a chemical and energy company in South Africa, Mozambique, the United States, Europe, and internationally. It offers bitumen, industrial heating fuels, naphtha, lubricants and lubricant base oils, liquefied petroleum gas, automotive and industrial lubricants, greases, cleansers and degreasers, automotive fuels, and burner fuels, as well as illuminating paraffin transport fuels, such as petrol, diesel, and jet fuels. The company also provides methane rich and natural gas; leaners and degreasers; hydrocarbon liquid fuel; specialty gas, butane, and propane; gasoline, kerosene (jet fuel), olefins, alcohols, polymers, solvents, surfactants, co-monomers, ammonia, methanol, crude tar acids, sulphur, and fuel oil; gas to liquid fuel; sustainable aviation fuel; and other fuels, as well as engages in the wholesale of motor fuels. In addition, it is involved in engineering, research and development, and technology transfer; management of cash resources, investments, and procurement of loans; development and implementation of international gas to liquid and CTL ventures; marketing of fuels and lubricants; production, trading, and transportation of oil products, petrochemicals and chemical products, and derivatives; and coal mining activities. The company serves adhesives, agriculture and forestry, automotive and transportation, aviation, burner fuels, chemicals, construction and materials, corrosion protection, electrical and electronics, flavors and fragrances, furniture, health and medical, household and consumer goods, industrial products, lubricants, manufacturing, mining, packaging, paints and coatings, personal care, pharmaceuticals, plastics and polymers, publishing and inks, pulp and paper, rubber and tires, specialty graphite, steel and foundry, textile and leather, water treatment, and other industries. Sasol Limited was founded in 1950 and is based in Sandton, South Africa.

financial_summary: Sasol Ltd. is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $7.7B market cap on $14.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -9% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $735M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.96× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.3) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Revenue growth lags most Basic Materials peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 164% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 34% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 56% and a beta of 0.81, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.13 vs 5y 0.66), so read it loosely.

val: The stock trades 41% below its DCF fair value of $20.18, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.96 to $52.04 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 10.8 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 1.4 vs 7.9 and P/FCF 10.5 vs 21.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 5% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 9.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $19.75 on average, 65% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 21.08).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 4.96x.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 9pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($2.2B of cash against $5.6B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.0x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.33 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -8.9% over 3 years and 2.3% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 96% of profits supports about 5.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -17.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Analysts expect -19.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 5%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $534K sold).
The share count has grown 0.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 26,943 employees, each generates about $524K of revenue, 0.8x the Basic Materials median.
That works out to $27K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (5x revenue per employee).
